Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . rewritten: The European lobster, scientifically known as Homarus gammarus, is a species of clawed lobster that inhabits the eastern Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, and certain parts of the Black Sea. It shares a close genetic relationship with the American lobster, H. americanus. Mature European lobsters can reach lengths of up to 60 cm (24 in) and weigh up to 6 kilograms (13 lb), characterized by their distinctive pair of claws. While alive, these crustaceans typically display a blue coloration, which only changes to a vibrant "lobster red" hue upon cooking. The mating process typically occurs during the summer months, resulting in female lobsters carrying eggs for approximately one year before they hatch into planktonic larvae. As a highly prized food source, European lobsters are primarily caught using lobster pots, mainly in the waters surrounding the British Isles.

The European lobster, Homarus gammarus, is a significant crustacean, measuring up to 60 centimeters in length and weighing between 5-6 kilograms. However, the lobsters typically caught in traps are usually shorter, ranging from 23-38 centimeters and weighing between 1.5-4.9 kilograms. Like other crustaceans, lobsters possess a hard exoskeleton that they must shed through a process called ecdysis, or moulting, in order to grow. Young lobsters may undergo this process several times a year, whereas larger individuals tend to molt only once every 1-2 years.

The initial pair of pereiopods is equipped with a distinctive, asymmetrical arrangement of claws. The larger and more robust claw is the "crusher," featuring rounded nodules that facilitate the crushing of prey, whereas the smaller, sharper claw is the "cutter," boasting inner edges designed for grasping or tearing food. Typically, the left claw assumes the role of the crusher, while the right claw serves as the cutter.

The exoskeleton of lobsters typically displays a blue hue on top, with spots that merge together, and a yellow underside. Interestingly, the red color often associated with lobsters is not naturally present; instead, it emerges only after cooking. This phenomenon occurs because, in their natural state, the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex. However, when subjected to heat, this complex breaks down, releasing the astaxanthin and revealing the red color.

The most closely related species to the European spider crab, H. gammarus, is the American lobster, Homarus americanus. These two species exhibit remarkable similarities, and it is feasible to cross-breed them artificially. However, it is unlikely that hybrids would occur naturally, as their geographical ranges do not overlap. To distinguish between the two species, several distinct characteristics can be employed.

Female Gammarus crabs typically reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80-85 millimeters (3 1/16 to 3 3/16 inches), whereas males mature slightly earlier. During the summer, mating usually occurs between a newly molted female, whose shell is still soft, and a hard-shelled male. After mating, the female carries the eggs for up to 12 months, depending on the temperature, attached to her pleopods. Females carrying eggs are referred to as "berried" and can be found throughout the year.

At dusk, the eggs of the species emerge, and the newly hatched larvae begin their journey to the ocean's surface, where they are carried by the currents and feed on zooplankton. This developmental stage, which involves three molting cycles, typically lasts between 15 to 35 days. As they shed their skins for the third time, the young larvae take on a physical appearance more similar to that of the adult, and they adapt to a benthic lifestyle. Unfortunately, very little is known about this phase in the wild, as the juveniles are rarely observed. However, it is believed that they are capable of excavating extensive burrows. Statistically, only about one larva in every 20,000 survives to reach this benthic phase. When they reach a carapace length of approximately 15 millimeters (0.59 inches), the juveniles leave their burrows and embark on their adult life.

The European lobster, Homarus gammarus, has a wide distribution across the north-eastern Atlantic Ocean, ranging from northern Norway to the Azores and Morocco, with the exception of the Baltic Sea. Additionally, it can be found in most parts of the Mediterranean Sea, excluding the area east of Crete, and along the north-western coast of the Black Sea. Notably, the species is also present in the Norwegian fjords, which are situated within the Arctic Circle, representing its northernmost populations.

The species can be categorized into four distinct genetic populations, with one widespread population and three others that have diverged due to small effective population sizes, potentially resulting from adaptation to their local environments. The northern Norway lobster population, often referred to as the "midnight sun lobster," is one such distinct population. Notably, the populations in the Mediterranean Sea differ from those in the Atlantic Ocean, and a separate population is found in the Netherlands, with samples collected from this region exhibiting distinct genetic profiles compared to those from the North Sea and English Channel.

Efforts have been undertaken to introduce the European lobster, H. gammarus, to New Zealand, alongside other non-native European species like the edible crab (Cancer pagurus). Between 1904 and 1914, a significant number of lobster larvae - approximately one million - were released from hatcheries in Dunedin, with the intention of establishing a viable population. However, despite these endeavors, the species failed to successfully establish itself in the region.

The adult H. gammarus inhabit the continental shelf, typically dwelling at depths ranging from 0 to 150 meters (492 feet) below the surface, with the majority of them found in the upper 50 meters (160 feet). These crustaceans prefer to reside on hard substrates, such as rocky outcroppings or compact mud, where they often burrow into holes and crevices. Notably, they venture out at night to forage for food, making the most of this brief window to satisfy their nutritional needs.

The European lobster (Homarus gammarus) is vulnerable to a disease caused by a specific bacterium. Although the disease is commonly found in American lobsters, it has only been observed in captive H. gammarus populations, where it is possible that the tanks had previously been occupied by American lobsters (H. americanus), making it difficult to rule out this factor as a contributing factor.

The Norway lobster, Homarus gammarus, is a prized food item with a rich cultural heritage, even featuring in a 17th-century English folk song. It commands a high price and can be sold in various forms, including fresh, frozen, canned, and powdered. Both the claws and abdomen of H. gammarus offer excellent white meat, and most parts of the cephalothorax are edible, with the notable exceptions of the gastric mill and sand vein (gut). Notably, the European species is considered to have a superior flavor, justifying its higher price point, which can be up to three times that of the American species, Homarus americanus.

Lobsters are primarily caught using lobster traps, although occasionally, lines baited with octopus or cuttlefish can entice them to swim out, allowing for capture in a net or by hand. According to 2008 statistics, a total of 4,386 tons of European lobster (H. gammarus) were caught across Europe and North Africa, with a significant proportion of 3,462 tons (79%) landed in the British Isles, including the Channel Islands. The minimum size limit for harvested European lobsters is a carapace length of at least 87 mm (3.4 inches).

H. gammarus is the designated type species of the genus Homarus Weber, established by International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature's Direction 51. Prior to this directive, the species was referred to by multiple names, including Astacus marinus Fabricius (1775) and Homarus vulgaris H. Milne-Edwards (1837), leading to confusion. Additionally, Friedrich Weber's original description of the genus was overlooked until Mary Rathbun's rediscovery, rendering any earlier designations of type species for Homarus H. Milne-Edwards (1837) invalid for Homarus Weber (1795).

The lectotype of Homarus gammarus, designated by Louis B. Holthuis in 1974, originated from a location near Marstrand, Sweden, which is approximately 30 miles or 48 kilometers northwest of Gothenburg at coordinates 57°53′N 11°32′E. Unfortunately, both the lectotype and the specimens have since been lost.

Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, a distinguished commander in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF), was born on July 15, 1914, and passed away on December 23, 1976. Headlam joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 and pursued a career in flying instruction and navigation before the onset of World War II. In April 1941, he took charge of No. 2 Squadron, which operated Lockheed Hudsons, and led the unit to Dutch Timor in December of the same year. The squadron engaged in combat operations against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific. Upon returning to Australia in February 1942, Headlam held various staff positions and training commands, culminating in his rank of group captain by the war's end.

Headlam held key positions within the Royal Air Force, including Officer Commanding North Western Area in 1946 and Director of Training from 1947 to 1950. During the Malayan Emergency, he commanded No. 90 (Composite) Wing and RAF Tengah in Singapore from 1950 to 1951. He also served as acting Air Member for Personnel twice, in 1957 and 1959-1960, and was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. With his promotion to air vice marshal, Headlam went on to hold various senior roles, including Air Officer Commanding Operational Command from 1961-1962, AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965-1966, and AOC Support Command from 1966-1967. He was honored as a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965. Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971, Headlam retired from the Air Force and passed away in Melbourne five years later.

Frank Headlam, the son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda, was born on July 15, 1914, in Launceston, Tasmania. He attended <unk> College in Hobart, Tasmania, and graduated in 1932. Against his parents' wishes, Headlam joined the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934. He then underwent flying instruction at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) in RAAF Point Cook, Victoria, and was commissioned as a pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

Following the completion of his conversion course, Headlam was posted to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook, where he was part of No. 1 Flight Training School. The squadron operated a range of aircraft, including Supermarine Southamptons and de Havilland Gipsy Moths, as well as other types. During this assignment, Headlam was promoted to flying officer on July 1, 1935, and authored a paper on national defense. In the paper, he proposed that a strong air force, naval force, including submarines, and fixed defenses could make Australia almost impregnable. According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens, this paper effectively laid the groundwork for the "anti-landing" concept, a strategic thinking paradigm that has persisted within the RAAF.

In July 1936, Headlam completed a flying instructors course and joined the staff at No. 1 FTS. He was promoted to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. In July 1938, he was one of six students to participate in the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course, led by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. The course consisted of extensive training flights that garnered significant media attention, including a 12-day, 10,800-kilometer (6,700-mile) round-Australia trip by three Avro Ansons, with Headlam piloting one of the planes in November. The following month, he led the three Ansons on a six-day journey back and forth over Central Australia. Headlam successfully completed the navigation course with special distinction. On January 27, 1939, he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, as a flight commander. Initially, he served with No. 2 Squadron, before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on August 29, 1939. Both units operated Ansons.

During World War II, No. 1 Squadron was responsible for escorting convoys and conducting maritime reconnaissance missions off the southeastern coast of Australia. Headlam remained a flight commander with the squadron until January 15, 1940, when he was transferred to Headquarters Laverton to serve as the station navigation officer. On March 27, he joined the staff of RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. Shortly after, on June 1, 1940, he was promoted to squadron leader. Two weeks later, on June 15, Headlam married Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston, with whom he would go on to have a son and a daughter.

Wing Commander Headlam took command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on April 15, 1941, and was promoted to his current rank on July 1. The squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, primarily conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until December 5, when four aircraft were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory, in response to concerns about Japanese aggression in the Pacific. On December 7, a detachment of four Hudsons established itself at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the remaining eight aircraft remained at Darwin on standby. The following day, one of the Penfui-based Hudsons attacked the Japanese ship Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a radio vessel, and forced it aground. By December 12, Headlam had transferred to Penfui, assuming command of both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, No. 2 Squadron's aircraft were stationed at Penfui, Timor Island, and Darwin. The detachment at Penfui targeted Japanese vessels participating in the invasion of Celebes. On January 11, two Hudsons successfully shot down or damaged three Japanese floatplanes that were attacking a transport ship during a bombing mission. However, the following day, both Hudsons were shot down by Mitsubishi Zeros. For the first time, Penfui was bombed by the Japanese on January 26, and it was subsequently attacked regularly, causing damage to some aircraft. The intact Hudsons were relocated to Darwin, while Headlam and his team remained at Penfui to enable the base to be used for reconnaissance missions from Australia. On February 18, Headlam was ordered to evacuate all personnel except a small team to demolish the airfield with the assistance of Sparrow Force. He returned to Darwin the next day, just as the city experienced its first Japanese raid. Four of No. 2 Squadron's Hudsons were destroyed in the attack, and the remaining aircraft were relocated to Daly Waters, where they continued to conduct reconnaissance and bombing missions against Japanese targets in Timor.

Headlam continued to serve in Darwin as the Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command until May 12, 1942, when he was reassigned to Nhill, Victoria, to lead No. 2 Air Navigation School, which operated Anson aircraft. The personnel of the school were used to form No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron in June. Headlam took command of No. 2 Air Observer School at Mount Gambier, South Australia, on July 20, 1943, where Ansons were also in use. He was promoted to Group Captain on December 1, 1943, and became the inaugural commander of No. 3 Squadron, operating Ansons and Fairey Battles out of Port Pirie, on December 9. After handing over command of No. 3 Squadron, Headlam began his studies at RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. He was subsequently appointed as the senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command on January 12, 1945.

In January 1946, Headlam took on the role of Officer Commanding North Western Area, before being posted to Britain later that year. He attended the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover and served with RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Upon returning to Australia in November 1947, he became the Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. Two years later, Headlam was appointed to command No. 90 (Composite) Wing, succeeding Group Captain Paddy Heffernan. Based in Singapore at RAF Changi, No. 90 Wing oversaw RAAF units operating during the Malayan Emergency, including No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, flying Avro Lincolns, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, flying Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns conducted area bombing missions and targeted attacks, while the Dakotas were responsible for courier flights, VIP transport, medical evacuations, and airlifting troops and cargo across South East Asia and Malaya. Headlam suffered a minor injury on December 20, 1950, after a No. 38 Squadron Dakota he was co-piloting crashed due to engine failure during a supply drop in Pahang. On February 19, 1952, Headlam took on the role of senior air staff officer (SASO) at the Eastern Area Command in Penrith, New South Wales. During his tenure, the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) began transitioning its fleet to English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. This period also saw a significant organizational overhaul, as the Air Force shifted from a geographically-based command and control system to one focused on function, leading to the establishment of Home, Training, and Maintenance Commands. As a result, the Eastern Area Command, which was essentially an operational headquarters due to its control over numerous combat units, was reorganized as Home Command in October 1953. Headlam's exceptional abilities and dedication earned him an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1954 New Year Honours. He was promoted to acting air commodore in May and later appointed aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II, with the announcement made on October 7, 1954.

Air Commodore Headlam was promoted to his substantive rank on January 1, 1955. Later that year, he was stationed at RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London, where he went on to pursue studies at the prestigious Imperial Defence College the following year. Upon his return to Australia, Headlam served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra, a role he held twice - first from March 19 to October 21, 1957, and again from August 24, 1959, to March 28, 1960. During his tenure, he sat on the Air Board, the RAAF's governing body, and was also a member of a committee, chaired by businessman William John Allison, that examined defense service conditions. The committee's recommendations led to significant improvements, including a doubling of flight pay. Headlam also held other positions at the Department of Air, including Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959, during which he was in charge of the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. He was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 1958 Queen's Birthday Honours and, in May 1960, became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

In January 1961, Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command (OPCOM), the successor to Home Command, overseeing the direction of RAAF operational units. He took over as Air Officer Commanding (AOC) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April, and was subsequently promoted to air vice marshal on May 29th. In July 1962, he was stationed at RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya and, a week later, assumed the role of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore. His tenure as AOC OPCOM came to an end with the appointment of Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch. As AOC No. 224 Group, Headlam was responsible for regional air defense and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia, which officially began the following month. Following his divorce from his first wife in 1956, Headlam married Vernon Spence, a widowed social worker, at the Sydney registry office on January 20, 1964. He transferred command of No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley Norris on November 30th.

After returning to Australia, Headlam took on the role of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on January 26, 1965. He was honored with the Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on June 22 for his exceptional service in the Borneo territories. During his tenure as DCAS, the Air Force embarked on its largest rearmament program since World War II, and manpower shortages arose due to this expansion and Australia's growing involvement in Southeast Asia's security. Towards the end of his term, the RAAF's first helicopters were deployed to the Vietnam War, and Headlam traveled to Saigon with Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton in March 1966 to plan the deployment. The previous year, Wilton had suggested sending two Iroquois to Vietnam for familiarization purposes, but Chief of the Air Staff Air Marshal Murdoch rejected the idea, leaving the RAAF's helicopter squadron underprepared for its army cooperation role. Headlam succeeded Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as Air Officer Commanding Support Command in Melbourne on August 8, 1966. This command was formed in 1959 by merging the RAAF's former Training and Maintenance Commands. On January 1, 1968, Headlam was posted to London as the head of the Australian Joint Services Staff. He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from November 17, 1970,

Following his return to Australia in June 1971, Headlam took a period of resettlement leave prior to his official retirement from the Air Force on August 3rd. He eventually settled in Melbourne, where he spent his remaining years. Unfortunately, he succumbed to a long and arduous battle with cancer, passing away at the age of 62 on December 23rd, 1976. At the time of his passing, he was survived by his children and his second wife. A private funeral was held, culminating in his cremation at the Springvale Crematorium.

Michigan State Trunkline M @-@ 82 spans the Lower Peninsula, connecting Fremont and Howard City. The route traverses Newaygo and Manistee National Forest, situated along its southern edge. Interestingly, this is the second iteration of M @-@ 82, with the first appearing in the Upper Peninsula as early as 1919. The Lower Peninsula route has been in use since the 1920s, although its terminus has undergone changes due to extensions and truncations, sometimes reaching as far west as New Era or Hesperia. The current route was finalized in the late 1970s, marking the end of the route's evolution.

Michigan Highway 82 begins at a pivotal intersection with Highway 120 and Business Highway 96, situated west of Fremont. This junction lies at the confluence of county lines, with Highway 120 forming the northern boundary between Newaygo, Oceana, and Muskegon counties, and Business Highway 96 running east-west along the Oceana-Muskegon county line. From this intersection, Highway 82 heads east, traversing rural farmland along 48th Street before entering the community of Fremont, where it becomes Main Street. The highway passes through the downtown area and turns south onto Stewart Avenue, exiting the town. The road then curves and transitions to 72nd Street, continuing eastward through more farm land. As the highway approaches Newaygo, the terrain becomes increasingly wooded, particularly near the Muskegon River. Highway 82 follows Fremont Street east to an intersection with Highway 37, merging and running concurrently over the river and into downtown along State Street. South of downtown, Highway 82 turns east again, independent of Highway 37, and runs along 82nd Street on the southern edge of the Manistee National Forest. The eastern terminus of Highway 82 is at exit 118 on US 131/Highway 46, located west of Howard City.

As part of its routine maintenance duties, the Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) monitors traffic volumes on its roadways. This data is presented in the form of average annual daily traffic (AADT), which represents the average number of vehicles using a specific stretch of road on any given day. According to MDOT's 2009 measurements, a segment of M-82 west of Fremont boasted the highest traffic volume, with approximately 16,532 vehicles daily. In contrast, the lowest traffic count was recorded at 4,018 vehicles east of Newaygo. Notably, MDOT has not designated any section of the highway as part of the National Highway System, a critical network of roads that supports the nation's economy, defense, and mobility.

The current M-82 route has its origins dating back to 1926, when it was established between Hart and Howard City, running concurrently with US-131 and M-46. The highway traversed through the towns of Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, replacing an earlier route, M-41. In 1936, M-46 was extended to fill a gap, creating a temporary concurrency with M-82 between Newaygo and Howard City. This merged section was later shortened to just M-46 in 1938, reverting M-82 to its original route north of Newaygo. A realignment of the highway west of Ferry took place in 1947 or 1948, and instead of terminating in Hart, the route was extended westward to Shelby.

In 1963 and 1964, the western section of the highway underwent two realignments, shifting its course from Hesperia to New Era, bypassing Ferry. A significant overhaul around 1969 reorganized the highway designations in Oceana County. M-20 replaced M-82 west of Hesperia, terminating at New Era instead of Muskegon, while M-120 took over the designation south of Hesperia. M-82 was subsequently rerouted from Hesperia to Newaygo only. The highway's length expanded in 1973 when its eastern end was relocated back to Howard City. M-46 was redirected to follow the US 131 freeway south of Howard City to Cedar Springs, supplanting M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This freed up the Newaygo-to-Howard City route for its reinstatement as M-82. The final modification occurred in 1978, when the concurrency with M-120 was eliminated in favor of the latter, and the M-82 designation was truncated to its current junction west of Fremont.

Shikamaru Nara is a fictional character in the Naruto manga and anime series created by Masashi Kishimoto. Despite being exceptionally intelligent, Shikamaru is often depicted as a laid-back character who is reluctant to utilize his full potential. Kishimoto has mentioned that he enjoys Shikamaru's easygoing nature, which sets him apart from other characters. Outside of the Naruto anime and manga series, Shikamaru has appeared in four feature films and various other media, including video games and original video animations.

Shikamaru's character has been extensively discussed in various anime and manga publications. Critics have highlighted his notable traits of laziness and exceptional intelligence, as well as his remarkable growth into a leader. Anime News Network praised his transformation, labeling him an "unlikely hero" in the Naruto narrative. Additionally, Shikamaru has gained immense popularity among Naruto fans, consistently ranking high in reader polls. As a result, numerous merchandise items featuring Shikamaru have been released, including action figures, keychains, and patches.

Masashi Kishimoto has expressed admiration for Shikamaru's affable personality, which belies his exceptional intellect. This characteristic stands in contrast to Sasuke Uchiha's intelligent yet abrasive demeanor. The creator has also joked that, if Shikamaru were a girl, he would marry him, attributing his character's potential success in life to his easygoing nature. When designing Shikamaru's appearance in Part II, Kishimoto aimed to give him a distinct look, despite the vest's similarity to those worn by other ninjas in the series. To achieve this, he decided to place the forehead protector on Shikamaru's arm, ensuring his hair remained visible.

Shikamaru's initial appearance in the series is during the Chunin Exams, a biennial evaluation for ninja seeking to advance in rank. He is part of Team 10 alongside two other team members, Ino Yamanaka, and an unnamed individual. Shikamaru is characterized by his apathetic nature, striving to go through life with minimal effort. However, his intellect is remarkable, with his teacher, Asuma Sarutobi, determining his IQ to be over 200. Shikamaru's abilities are centered around the Shadow Imitation Technique (Kagemane no Jutsu, dubbed "Shadow Possession Jutsu" in English), a signature technique of his clan, which allows him to merge his shadow with that of an opponent, rendering them immobile and forcing them to mimic his movements. As the series progresses, Shikamaru develops the ability to manipulate his shadow in various ways. By the time of Part II, he can utilize multiple shadow-based techniques simultaneously and lift his shadow from the ground to interact with physical objects, such as piercing enemies with shadow tendrils or using them to throw weapons.

Shikamaru enters the exams with a distinct lack of enthusiasm; however, he proves himself to be a formidable opponent when he faces off against Temari, a skilled ninja from Sunagakure. Despite emerging victorious, Shikamaru chooses to forfeit the match due to his dwindling chakra reserves. Although he does not win the match, his exceptional strategic thinking and intelligence impress the exam administrators, leading to his promotion to the rank of Chunin. As a newly appointed Chunin, Shikamaru is entrusted with the responsibility of leading a team tasked with preventing Sasuke Uchiha from defecting to Otogakure. Although his team successfully defeats the Otogakure ninja attempting to intercept them, Sasuke ultimately manages to evade capture and escape.

In the subsequent episodes of the series, Shikamaru is tasked with tracking down two members of the notorious Akatsuki organization. Despite his team's efforts, they manage to locate their targets, but the immortal Akatsuki member, <unk>, ultimately proves too powerful, killing Asuma Sarutobi in the ensuing battle. Grief-stricken, Shikamaru joins forces with Kakashi Hatake and the surviving members of Team 10 to avenge their fallen mentor. While his comrades confront <unk>'s partner, Shikamaru single-handedly defeats and disposes of <unk>'s body, vowing to protect Kurenai and Asuma's newborn daughter. Following this ordeal, Shikamaru is assigned to the Fourth Division alongside Temari and <unk>, and is named a proxy general under Gaara. In the series' epilogue, Shikamaru reveals his personal aspirations, becoming an advisor to the Seventh Hokage Naruto after marrying Temari and having a son, <unk> Nara.

Additionally, Hiroshi Matsuyama, CEO of CyberConnect2, has publicly expressed his fondness for Shikamaru, naming him as one of his favorite characters from the Naruto franchise.

Various publications covering manga, anime, and video games have discussed the character of Shikamaru. IGN regarded him as one of their favorite characters, labeling him the "poster child for any card-carrying member of Generation X" due to his lack of enthusiasm and reluctance to utilize his abilities.
